cells.tense: You are here with your hands on this, tending what's yours and clearing it as it finishes.
cells.ask: Pick one shared thing that has stopped producing — a shelf, a chat, a slot — and clear it yourself this week. End it out loud, so it's done rather than drifted.
cells.core:
You're tending what's yours while it's still alive, and clearing it out when it's finished. Not forcing either one — when a thing has run its course, you can put it down. That includes the parts other people count on you to keep going, and you make that call without a scene. You close things so the next thing can start. That's the whole work of this ground, and you're standing in it.
What it costs to keep this: endings stay quiet, because you'd rather clear than explain. Someone near you may not know a door closed. Say a clean sentence about one thing you've finished, and it stays finished more clearly.

cells.verb: Tending what grows, and clearing the ground when it's done

cells.tense: You are bracing for an ending that hasn't arrived, clearing things ahead of their time.
cells.ask: Before you finish anything this week, ask what's actually inside it — a shift in timing, a bad day — and let the thing stand one more week.
cells.core:
You're clearing ground that isn't finished. Reading ahead for what's about to break, ending things a beat early so the end can't surprise you. From the outside it looks decisive, but from inside it's effort — you're managing every ending before the moment gets its turn. The care that was easy has started to cost, because the hands that tend a thing are also watching for its last breath.
What's being skipped isn't the ending. It's the time a thing needs to be what it is first. When release comes from something that actually completed, it doesn't feel like defeat. It feels like the end of a sentence. Before you put one down, sit with what it still is for an hour.

cells.tense: You are still standing in a doorway from before, with your hands not quite tending anything.
cells.ask: Open something you've stopped opening — one file, one drawer, one project you used to run — and do fifteen minutes of the old tending. Not to decide anything, just to touch it.
cells.core:
An ending is still waiting to be walked through, and it went on so long that you've stopped tending. It looks like peace from the outside: quiet, not building. But the hands that used to grow things have gone still, and the room around it feels like a waiting room rather than a finished one. This isn't about needing a visible ending. It's that your sense of what you can carry is still out of date.
Tend one small thing that used to matter, and the ground you buried comes back in reach. Nobody has to be told what it was. Growth without forcing, care that doesn't exhaust — that's what you're rebuilding, one small act at a time.

cells.tense: You are already being tended and structured by something in you, and you're calling it circumstances.
cells.ask: Name one arrangement you've been calling "the situation" and say what you did to keep it running — one true sentence. Once, to yourself or someone who'll just take it.
cells.core:
Something in you tends the small things without asking you: you water it, you arrange it, you keep it running. That version is steady and unattended — the plant gets watered, the schedule holds, nobody has to be told. Right now you talk about it like it's the room's doing, or theirs. The care is real. People feel it in how you keep a thing upright.
What's missing isn't the effort. It's the claim. Say out loud that you're the one who keeps this going, and the hands that have been working without a name get one. That authority is the whole turn. It only sits on the person who did the work. Take yours back from the furniture.
